record.Etymology: 4. Kurkh. teṅgnā (tiṅgyas) ‘to tell, narrate, explain’, Malt. tenge ‘to tell, point out, relate’ (DEDR 3409) — Sre ntiŋ ‘to tell, to charge a commission’, Tampuan tɛɛŋ ‘tell, speak about’ and taiŋ ‘tell, speak about’, Palaung taiŋ ‘to speak’.

record.Gloss: curds mixed with salt, chillies, mustard, etc., and some rice flour boiled and seasoned
record.Etymology: 287. Kal. kaḍí, kạí ‘gravy made from meat juices and flour’ is cognate with OIA (Suśr.) khaḍa-, khala- ‘buttermilk boiled with acid vegetables and spices’ (3783). Origin is unclear, but Mayrhofer (EWA) correctly refers to possible Dravidian origin; cf. e.g. Kan. kaḍi ‘curds mixed with salt, chillies, mustard, etc., and some rice flour boiled and seasoned’ (DEDR 1128).

accepted.evidence: DEDR1128 explicitly records Kannada kaḍi with the same detailed prepared-curds gloss. Zoller p.557 cites1128 accurately. This is a direct family match; the possible Dravidian origin of the surrounding Indo-Aryan forms is a separate claim.

record.Etymology: 300. Kann. kár ‘sheep’, Rp. kar ‘ram; billy goat’, Bun. kar ‘sheep (male, castrated)’ — cf. Ind. kʌ́rū ‘lion, tiger; wild sheep’ with many parallels in languages in the northwest (loc.cit.); also Kann. byaṅ kar(h) ‘Tibetan ram’, Par. ɣarȭ ‘sheep’, Sak. kaura- ‘sheep’, Wkh. kar ‘mouton à courtes oreilles’, Bur. kíro ‘sheep (child’s language)’, karéelo ‘ram’, Sh.chil. kará̄ ‘a ram’ — Bhil. karᵃḍu and M. karaḍũ̄ both ‘kid’. As I have pointed out (2005: 103) the word might be of Dravidian origin, e.g., Tam. koṟi ‘sheep’ (cf. DEDR 1799 for Dravidian alloforms and semantic varieties similar to those of Northern Pakistan), whereas Harold Walter Bailey suggests derivation < PIE *kapro- ‘he-goat’ (1979: 65). But cf. also Čašule’s suggestion (e.g. 2010: 44) for a PIE background which he supports with reference to Bur. karóoỵo and Sh. karóovo ‘with curved horns’.

accepted.evidence: DEDR2165(a) explicitly records Tamil koṟi sheep and ends with the older DED(S)1799 concordance. Zoller p.558 labels1799 as DEDR, but current DEDR1799 concerns roots/tubers. Match the attested sheep family2165; preserve the printed citation in the source record without endorsing surrounding Indo-European comparisons.

record.Etymology: 3. Bng. poet. ɔḷɔ1 ‘soft’ — Ind. ʌ̀l ‘soft’, K. öyⁱlᵘ ‘very soft’. Cf. Tam. aḷi ‘to become mellow’ (DEDR 257).

accepted.evidence: DEDR302 explicitly gives Tamil aḷi become mellow, be over-boiled and the older DED257 concordance. Zoller p.746 labels257 as DEDR, whose actual article is an iron-wood tree. The exact form and sense support302; no tree-family link is proposed.

record.Etymology: 67. Bng. tɔpkāṇɔ v.t. ‘to grope one’s way, grope along’ (with -k- and -a- suffixes), tɔprāḷ n.m. ‘groping step(s) that lead towards a goal’ (with -rāḷ suffix) and probably tɔpɔ n.m. ‘place or goal within reach, reach, range’, top(i)ṇɔ ‘to guess, figure, feel, touch’ (note topuiɔ pɔriaṇṇɔ ‘to make out or identify by touch or feeling’ [first verb is ABS, second < prájānāti ‘knows, understands’ 8509a]) and pɔrtɔpṇɔ ‘to feel around, grope about’ (with pɔr- prefix), Khaśdh. topiṇa and Deog. tōpṇɔ ‘to grope along’, Old Cam. tōpṇā ‘to look for’, Kann. taptapyá-mig (tap-ta-pyá-mig) ‘to touch, to search for by the touch, to feel or grope for, to seek by feeling’, Pāḍ. and Maṇḍ. tōpṇᵃ ‘to search’ — Ind. tʌ̀p-tʌpʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to tap, touch lightly’, Bur./Sh. taptáp -̇t- ‘to tap on; tippen an’, and aspirated Ind. thʌ́p-thʌpʰ karʌ́ṽ ‘to grope or feel around in darkness’, Sh.chil. tháp-thap th- ‘to grope around in darkness’, Sh.koh. (RSup) thapȭ vakhat ‘evening’ (second word ← Ar. vaqt ‘time’), Bro. tʰʌptʰup ‘dark’. The aspirated Dard forms appear to be partly contaminated by OIA *thapp- ‘slap, pat’ (6091) – but note also Proto-Khasic *tʰaap ‘to hit, slap’ – whereas the unaspirated WPah. forms may have a parallel in Tam. tappu- ‘to grope, feel about’ (DEDR 2499). We are probably dealing here with a ‘North Indian’ word. Therefore see the following note: Note: A here perhaps related subgroup is this: Pur. ṭʰup ‘dark’ — cf. Bur. ṭumṭáṅ ‘darkness with (or through) dust’ if < older *ṭupṭáṅ (with second sylla- ble ṭaṅ ‘(sky) covered, cloudy, rainy’) — with Bur. are related Sant. ʈamɖao ‘to grope, to feel with hands or feet, as in the dark or in water, to search or try to find in the dark or in water’ (related with ʈamɖa ʈəmɖi ‘to grope, or feel here and there’ and Korwa ʈamɖaːo ‘to grope in the dark’ both of which possibly go back to older *ʈap-) and probably ʈahuʔp ʈaʈuʔp ‘stumbling, floundering, as one walking in the dark; to go slap dash’ (which might derive from older *ʈaʈuʔp ʈaʈuʔp).

accepted.evidence: DEDR3072 explicitly gives Tamil tappu grope, feel about and the older DED(S)2499 concordance. Zoller p.757 labels2499 as DEDR, whose actual article means quickly. Preserve the source boundary hyphen; link the full grope family3072 without adopting the wider North Indian comparison.

record.Etymology: 145. Ind. mʌ̀ṽ ‘a riverbank; a landing place, moorings (at a river bank)’, Kamd. gāl-mól ‘river-bank’, Wg. golmalˈa ‘river bank, valley floor’ (with first word < OIA *ghala- ‘stream’ [4453]), Dm. khoi-má̄li ‘river-bank’ (with first word < OIA *khola- ‘cavity, hollow’ [3943]), Paš. nandə-mālˈa ‘river-bank’ (with first word < OIA nadí̄- ‘river’) and vargamˈāl ‘river-bank’ (with varg(a) < OIA vá̄ri- ‘water, rain’ [11556]) — Orm. ṣʳī-mōl ‘field-embankment’. According to Morgenstierne and accepted by Turner, the Paš. and Dm. forms are < OIA má̄lā- ‘wreath, garland’ (10092). But this is implausi- ble. Therefore alternatively the words derive < PIE *molā ‘shore’ (Pokorny and Köbler but not Mallory and Adams; cf. e.g. Latv. mala ‘edge, bank, border, shore, region’), however contamination by forms related with H. etc. moṛ ‘curve’ (< OIA [ultimately Dravidian móṭati ‘twists’] is possible, cf. Kal. moḷ ‘turn, bend’). Note: See also somewhat similar OIA malaya- and Tam. malai ‘hill, mountain’ (DEDR 4742). Because of Dravidian and Indo-European evidence, Bomhald reconstructs PN *mal-a ‘hill, mountain (CINCL 846). Note, however, also In- scriptional Sanskrit māla- ‘field’ and lex. ‘a forest or wood near a village’, Munda Bodo-Gadaba mala ‘hill field, land cleared for ploughing’ and the synonym form mal biroŋ ‘mountain range’ with further parallels in Mon-Khmer like Brao məːl ‘dry paddy field’, Sapuan mɨəl ‘rice field (wet & dry)’, Tˈin mual ‘plant rice in hill field’.

accepted.evidence: DEDR4742 explicitly records Tamil malai hill, mountain; Zoller pp.837–838 cites it accurately. This proposal identifies the attested Dravidian family only, without adopting the broader Indo-European or Nostratic interpretations in his discussion.

record.Etymology: 147. The following Bng. lemma has already been published (Zoller [1989: 195]), but here follows additional data: Bng. magu adj.,n.m. ‘a little but strong one (boy); a boy’ — Sh.ast. māgī ‘children’ (Nayyar [1986: 45]), cf. PIE *magʰus ‘young man’, but cf. also Sh. maági n.m. ‘darling (no sexual connotation)’ and PN *mag-a ‘young person, child; young’. Note, however, also Ta. maka ‘child, infant, young of animal, son or daughter, young age’ (DEDR 4616), Kan. maga ‘son, male person’, etc. Note: The genuine PIE origin of this ‘lemma’ has been questioned by several scholars, e.g. by Tatyana Mikhailova (2007: 16ff.) who postulates a merger of Nostratic *mVkV and PIE *maghu- ‘fellow, unmarried (p. 17), Ranko Matasović (2009 sub Proto-Celtic *makʷo- ‘son’) and Guus Kroonen (2013) who writes sub Proto-Germanic *magu- ‘boy, relative’ “[a] West European word of obscure origin.”

accepted.evidence: DEDR4616 explicitly records Kannada maga son, male person within the child/son family. Zoller p.839 supplies the same form and gloss with4616 governing the comparison. No Indo-European or Nostratic ancestry is asserted by this family link.

record.Etymology: 176. Bng. ùṛkɔ1 n.m. ‘a small drum’ (a word from the neighbouring area Seraĩ), Garh. and Ku. huṛkiya < OIA lex. huḍukka- ‘a kind of rattle or small drum’. Mayrhofer thinks the word is onomatopoeic and points also to Tu. uḍuku ‘a kind of small drum’ and Rāj. huḍukkā- perhaps ‘a kind of bagpipe’.

accepted.evidence: DEDR589 explicitly records Tulu uḍuku a kind of small drum, matching Zoller p.544. Its Sanskrit huḍukka comparison is not a specified borrowing direction. This proposal identifies the attested Dravidian article family while retaining the possibility of local transmission or expressive origin.

record.Etymology: 282. Words for cuckoo (or ‘cuckoo’ sounding words designating other birds) are certainly onomatopoeic. But this knockout argument does not mean too much. Within the northwestern and a few other Outer Languages they can be divided into a few groups, in this way disclosing some typological relationships. Note also that some languages have more than one word for ‘cuckoo’. (a) The OIA kokilá- type. The words of this group have not lost the medial -k- just like their Dravidian parallels: Pal. kaˈkūli ‘cuckoo’, Bhad. kākoli ‘cuckoo’ (Kaul [2006 i: 107]), Kaul also gives with- out further West Pahāṛī language specification (2006 i: 32) gaḍkākoli ‘cuckoo of the rivulet’ (but 2006 ii: 395 he says it is from Bhal. meaning ‘pakṣī viśeṣ – type of bird’); in vol. i p. 187 there is the additional alloform Bhal. gaḍ kagholi (with first syllable < OIA *gaḍḍa-¹ ‘hole’ [3981] and note k – gh alternation); there is also the Bng. cuss pũnskōklɔ ‘flatterer, idiot, blockhead’ which cf. with S. kokiḍī ‘stupid as a fowl’; Him. koklā ‘the blackbird’, N. kokʌle ‘cuckoo’ (Z.) and Western Nepal shamanic language kokalsārī ‘cuckoo’ — K. kukilü ‘cuckoo’, Ind. kʌkuìlⁱ ‘cuckoo’ and Bur.ys. káku, kúku ‘cuckoo’ (but note also p. 792 Bur. kápo ‘cuckoo’ and Bur.ys. kíki ‘falcon’) – Ko. koguḷ ‘cuckoo’. Cf. OIA kokilá- ‘cuckoo’ (3483), kukubha- ‘the wild cock Phasianus gallus’ (3210), *kūkkati ‘screams’ (3390), DN: 21 kokk-, kukk- ‘call’ and PMK *kuk, kuuk ‘to call’, but more significant are semantically close Dravidian parallels: Kan. kukil ‘cuckoo’, Tu. kogilè, kojilè ‘cuckoo’, etc. (b) The kuku type which does not have close Dravidian parallels: Kiũṭh. kūkū ‘cuckoo’, Jaun. kūkhū ‘cuckoo’, N. kukku ‘cuckoo’— K. kuku ‘cuckoo’ — Bhaṭ. bã̄kükú ‘type of brown-coloured pheasant’ with first component < vána-¹ ‘forest’ (11258) resembles K. van-kŏkürü ‘a kind of wild bird resembling a barndoor fowl’ but both may rather contain the word for ‘hen’ — Gau. kukʰ ‘type of woodpecker’, Bur.ys. kúku ‘cuckoo’, Kho. káku ‘cuckoo’ and narkˈuku ‘rooster’ (with first syllable < OIA nára- ‘male’ [6970]) — Jaṭ. kak ‘large hill partidge’ — Yid. kakūk ‘cuckoo’. Cf. PIE *kukū ‘cuckoo’. (c) kuku with other extensions: Sutlej Group koklas ‘type of pheasant’ (Malhans [2002: 262]) and Sh.dras. kʌ́kəs ‘pheasant’ (Rajapurohit [2012: 43]) are probably built on the kokilá- basis with vāśuka- element like other ‘pheasant’ words in the northwest (see p. 648 and Aw. kaṭnās ‘a kind of bird [? a jay]’ which may be a case of semantic-morphological amalgamation [on this term see p. 224]). N. kākākul ‘a part. kind of bird’ has a close parallel in Nuristani Kt. kúku kuli ‘cuckoo’ (cf. OIA *kululi- ‘outcry’ [3347]). Kal. kokḍúm ‘cuckoo-like bird’, Kho. kokdˈum ‘coocoo’ (‘cuckoo’) with unclear second component. Rp. kəkcilāṛu ‘a black chicken-like bird’ is a synonym compound: cf. Bng. ċilāṛ ‘cuckoo’ with first syllable < OIA cilli- ‘a kind of bird of prey’ (4829) and Jaun. bhūĩ̄-cīl ‘pheasant’ (with first word < OIA bhú̄mi- ‘earth, ground’ [9557]). More unclear are Psht. kūkūkūtarah ‘a ringdove’ (probably kūkū plus kotar ‘pigeon’), and Mult. and P. kakuhā ‘sandpiper’.

accepted.evidence: DEDR1764 explicitly records Tulu kōgilè and kōjilè cuckoo; Zoller pp.555–556 prints the same variants with short o. Keep that quantity difference explicit. The dictionary also compares Sanskrit kokila and Zoller calls these bird names onomatopoeic; the family proposal does not establish independent inheritance or a donor route.

record.Etymology: 519. (a) Bng. cəś ‘burning pain’, Kc. ċaśiṇo ‘to be burnt (e.g. hand on hot iron)’, Deog. and Jaun. ciśṇɔ ‘to burn one’s hand etc.’, Him. cośṇu ‘to burn with fire’, P. cīs ‘a sharp pain’, Ku. ciśṇō ‘to burn’, ciśi ‘scare of fire’ and cis ‘keen pain, scorching’, cisuk ‘very cold’, N. ciso ‘wet, cold’, Kgr. cas ‘slipped disc’ — Ind. c̣ʌ̀ṣ ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain; lumbago; a touch’ and c̣ʌ̀s ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain’, Kal. čičiék ‘to burn or smart (as salt in a wound)’. The words are to be seen in connection (i) with OIA *cassakk- ‘throb, twitch, sudden pain’ (4730), *cīssa- ‘sharp pain’ (4847), caṣati² ‘hurts’ (4727a), chaṣati ‘hurts’ (Dhātup.) (the aspirated form is reflected in Garh. chasāk ‘nukīlī vastu kī halkī cubhan - slight sting or piercing through a pointed object’), cahakk- ‘burn brightly’ (4731) (with debuccalisation), and perhaps cāṣa-  ‘sugarcane’ (4774) (see there G. cās ‘boiled syrup’), and (ii) with OIA *atyuṣati ‘burns’, *atyoṣati, *atyuṣyate ‘is burnt’ (226a), and (iii) perhaps with Dravidian DEDR kiccu (1514): Tam. kiccu ‘fire’, Tel. ciccu ‘fire, flame’ etc. which is perhaps worth comparing with Garh.nā. cac-kār, cac-gār ‘very cold’ (with -kār suffix). record.Etymology: 1244. Bng. mɔ̄ḷṇɔ, mɔḷmɔḷaṇɔ, ‘to glitter’ and miḷmiḷaṇɔ v.i. ‘to flicker (as light); to flash (lightning)’, kɔḷmɔḷi adj. and kɔḷmɔḷī n.f. ‘burning (as a sensation); shining, sparkling; shine, lustre, sparkle’ and here perhaps umbḷɛ̄ṇɔ v.i. ‘to flicker, waver (e.g., a fire, swarm of flies)’ (with -ɛ-, ɛ̄- suffix). The reduplicated form is found, e.g., in the PAN, describing the ‘flickering’ (i.e. light emitting) crown of King Duryodhana, e.g.: raza Duriodən kɔ barthɛ kɔ mukuṭ mɔḷmɔḷa King Duryodhana GEN.POP stately.OBL GEN.POP crown flickers ‘The stately crown of King Duryodhana flickers’[318] Cf. OIA (AV) kalmali- ‘splendour, brightness, sparkling’ and OIA malmalābhávant- ‘flashing, glittering’. For kalmali- Chandrasekaran (p. 41) suggests Dravidian origin, e.g. found in Tam. mallal ‘elegance, brilliance’, which cannot be the source for the Bng. word, but for which Bomhard suggests PN origin (< *mal-a ‘fullness’ [CINCL 847]). Mayrhofer says about malmalābhávant- (EWA II: 333) with reference to Karl Hoff- mann that the word is ‘sound symbolic rendering of a (visual?) impression (‘Gesichts- eindruck’) through repetitive onomatopoeia’, but Chandrasekaran (p. 42) suggests also for this word Dravidian origin and he quotes as parallels Parji melk- ‘to lighten’, malk- ‘(light) to flash’ and Pengo malkā- ‘to lighten’ (p. 41) which, however, have parallels in Indo-Aryan Ḍog. milk ‘lightning’, Dari. milkala ‘lightning’, N. milkinu ‘(of the sky) to flash with lightning’ and most variants of Ind. ˈmili ‘lightning’ (Hallberg [1992: 211]; Leitner [1889: appendix iv, 14]), Gau. milyõ ‘lightning’, K. vuzmal and Sir.ḍoḍ. uz- muliˈya ‘lightning’ (both are synonym compounds with first component (v)uz- < OIA vidyút- ‘flashing, lightning’ [11742]), and Tibeto-Burman Khm. milak ‘flash, flash of lightning’ and Western Tibetan Balt. melmel ci ‘a very small indistinct glow (of light)’. There is also the H. ideophone milmilānā ‘shine, shimmer, glitter’ (Kellersmann [2017: 609]). Thus, derivation < PIE *(s)mel- ‘give off light smoke, smoulder’ and possible contamination by ‘sound symbolic’ word forms is rather unlikely. Still, if the OIA form can be characterized as ‘repetitive onomatopoeia’ one wonders that it survived unchanged over millennia in a comparatively small area. Note also that the Bng. poet. word barthɔ ‘stately’ is hardly < OIA bhártr̥- ‘husband’ etc. (9402), displaying a rightward displacement of aspiration but rather cognate with bharatá-. However, cf. Pischel § 207 who mentions OIA suffix -tha instead of -ta in M., AMg., JM. Bhāraha. Note also Martirosyan’s perhaps related reconstruction (2013: 112) PIE *mar- mar- reflected in dialectal Arm. *mar-m(a)r-il ‘to shimmer, flicker, glimmer, ex- tinguish gradually (said of e.g. a candle)’ and Greek μαρμαίρω ‘to flash, sparkle, gleam’ (said of any darting, quivering light).

record.Etymology: 83. CAṬ) — cf. record.Etymology: 282. Words for cuckoo (or ‘cuckoo’ sounding words designating other birds) are certainly onomatopoeic. But this knockout argument does not mean too much. record.Etymology: 302. record.Etymology: 131. Byangsi śiṅram ‘ginger’, Chaudangsi ɕin-rəm ‘ginger’, Darma ɕiŋ-wəm ‘ginger’ and perhaps Chepang sim.phərʔ ‘ginger’ are most certainly not borrowings from OIA śr̥ṅgavera- ‘dried or fresh ginger’ (12588). Turner (CDIAL) and Mayrhofer (EWA) speculate about Dravidian connections (which is correct for -vera- which cf. with Tam. vēr ‘root’) and ultimate borrowing of a (South-)East Asian culture word. Yet, the Austro-Asiatic origin is quite obvious: Khasi sʔíːŋ ‘ginger’, Tˈin khɨːŋ ‘ginger’, Bolyu tɕiŋ⁵⁵ ‘ginger’, Riang kᵊsiaŋ¹ ‘ginger (Zingiber officinale)’ and Danaw kᵊʦɑŋ⁴ ‘ginger (Zingiber officinale)’ and Palaung siaŋ ‘ginger’, and Proto-Vietic *s-gəːŋ ‘ginger’. Byangsi -ram and Chaudangsi -rəm are the same as Darma rɯm ‘root’. Thus, the WH and the OIA forms have the same semantic structure ‘ginger-root’. Darma -wəm compares with Western Tani amya ‘root’ and different variants of the Zeme Group which have forms like ama, küman, pema all ‘root’ which suggest that WH -rəm, rɯm is basically a synonym compound ‘root-root’ with -r- perhaps related with Proto- Karenic #7445 PKar *rwiB ‘root’.

accepted.evidence: DEDR5535 explicitly records Tamil vēr root, anything rootlike, foundation. Zoller pp.915–916 quotes the independent Tamil root noun when discussing ginger compounds. This is the root family, not the homographic anger or sweating articles.

record.Etymology: 106. Pr. ẓugˈo ‘bell’, ẓugˈeig ‘bell; rushing or roaring of water’, ẓuṅulˈeig ‘small bell’ appear etymologically related with Kal. gạṅgạí ‘large bell (typically tied to the neck of a male goat or bull)’. We deal here obviously with ideophones for which *gruṅ-, *groṅ-, *graṅ- can be reconstructed — Nuristani Kt. gřaṅˈaři ‘bell’ — West Himalayish Bun. koroŋkoroŋ ‘a bell’ and Darma kɔloŋ ‘bell (a type)’, and also Bodo gugrá ‘bell (kind of, round, tied to the neck of a horse)’ is almost identical with below Santali. The forms are ultimately borrowings from Austro-Asiatic: — Sant. ghugra ‘morris bells, a band of small bells tied round the ankles when dancing’ and here perhaps also ghanar ghunur ‘tinkling, jingling (sound of small bells)’, Korku ghuruŋgula, guruŋgula ‘string of small bells worn by bullocks’ and koɽoŋ ‘round brass bell for cattle’ — Bahnar grɛŋ- nɛŋ ‘small bell’ and Cua graneŋ ∼ gareŋ ∼ reŋ ‘bell’, Halang gəgraʔ gəgri̤ːŋ ‘jingling of bells’ and griːŋ ‘the rings of a small bell’, Sre gruŋ ‘bell’, Ngeq krlooŋ ‘buffalo bell’, Khmu krlɛːŋ ‘metal bell around an animal’s neck’, Thavung kalɛŋ ‘a small cylindrically shape bell’, etc. Note: Derivation of the the Pr. and Kal. form < OIA *ghuṅghura- ‘bell’ (4477), for which Turner suggests borrowing from Dravidian which he supports by quot- ing Kan. gugguri ‘curl’, is unlikely. Here more or less (in)directly connected are also the following: H. ghanghan- ‘(bell) sound, jingle, clink’, OIA *ghanaghana- ‘tinkle, clang’ (4425) which is according to Turner and Mayrhofer onomatopoeic.

record.Etymology: 115. ‘Butterfly’ and ‘flying-fluttering’ (a) Deog. phiphṛi and phimphṛi ‘butterfly’, Kṭg. phímpəṛi ‘butterfly’ (wrongly put in the Addenda and Corrigenda sub pipīlá- ‘ant’ [8201]), Khaśdh. putuṛi ‘butterfly’, Ku. purputaī ‘butterfly’, Jaun. pōtōṭhō, Him. phĩphṛī, Khāśi. phāphṛi, Pāḍ. pāpṛi, Bhal. papṛi, pepri, Khaś. phāphṛi, Bhad. pāpṛi or pepṛõ all ‘butterfly’ — Kurkh. pəpəla ‘butterfly’ — Paṭṭ. phərphitig ‘butterfly’, Chin. pharphiṭig (or phārpitig, Kaul [2006 ii: 42]) ‘butterfly’, Gar. phremolig ‘butterfly’, K. pam pũ̄par ‘butterfly’ (Sachdeva et al. [2010: 60]) — Ind. phirphirì̄ ‘butterfly’, Bur. asqúriṅe phirán ‘butterfly’, Tor.cail. pʌrparʌk ‘moth’, Paš. pheṭiyák ‘butterfly’ — Psht. parkai ‘butterfly’ — Khet. phōpuṭ ‘butterfly’, S. popṭu ‘butterfly’, Jaṭ. popaṭ ‘butterfly, moth’ and bhabbaṭ ‘moth’, Ko.S. phulpã̄khrũ ‘butterfly’ (with second component < OIA pakṣín- ‘bird’), Ko.kaṇ. birbirẽ ‘butterfly’ — Sad. paplā ‘butterfly’ and Kh. pampla, phamphlaʔ which seems (like first word in K. pam pũ̄par) to have Austro-Asiatic parallels: Bahnaric Cua pʌm pil ‘moth, butterfly’, Proto-Vietic *paːmə ‘butterfly’, Sant. pipṛiaṅ ‘butterfly’ and Bon. laʔlaʔp ‘butterfly’, and Mon-Khmer LwAd. poopil ‘butterfly’. Perhaps also related are Kho. pulmuṇḍuk ‘butterfly’, Sh.gur. phōpal ‘butterfly’, Wkh. pilek-miˈlek or pilpilak ‘butterfly’ and Ishk. parparanuk ‘butterfly’, Kamd. prüšpˈulik ‘butterfly; moth’, Bal. pirrik ‘butterfly’. Cf. PIE *pelpel- ‘butterfly’, Latin pāpiliō, Arm. xipilik (loanword?), all ‘butterfly’; cf. also Common Kartvelian *perpel-‘butterfly; wing’, Zan (Laz dialect) parpal-i, Megrelian parpal-ia//parpal-i ‘butterfly; twisting/swirling’; cf. also PTB *pur ‘butterfly’ which, however, is not found in Tib., the only geographically plausible near form is Kann. pʰərpʰitig ‘butterfly’. Generally one can say that many of the above forms got not only ‘indianized’ i.e. they are examples for linguistic naturalization (on this term see p. 223), but also intersected with similar-sounding words e.g. from Austro-Asiatic and Dravidian, and last but not least some of the words may have also been influenced by reflexes of OIA pattrá- ‘wing’ with -ṭṭ- extension (7733) and by the following lemma (b). Cf. also Proto-Dravidian *papla ‘butterfly’ (Pfeiffer [1972: 20f.]) and e.g. Ora. paplā ‘butterfly’, and simimlar “sound-symbolism” forms in Munda (Kuiper [1962: 82]). (b) Bng., Deog. and West Pahāṛī far ‘the sound of a bird’s flight’, Khaśdh. phʌr-phʌr ‘ditto’, Garh. phurr ‘sound of a flying bird’ and pharṛī ‘a banner’, N. pharpharāhaṭ, phyār-phyār, pher-pher all ‘fluttering’ and Khm. phur phur ‘high in the air’, Rab. furut ‘sound of flying away a bird’ (Roy [2011: 100]) — Jaḍ. phur-phurja ‘to fly’ (Z.), Pur. phurcas ‘to fly’ (with infinitive/verbal noun ending), Balt., Nyam-kad and Tib. phur ‘(to) fly’ (other Tibetan forms are phir-, bur-, ur-), New. pharphar, phyār phyār ‘fluttering’ — Brah. firfir and paṛpaṛ ‘flutter; fluttering’ — Ind. phʌ́r ho- ‘to fly’, also in some Sh. dialects puř- and phuri- ‘fly’, Kho. pár ‘sound of bird’s wings flapping’, Bur.ys. pər ɛt- ‘to fly’ — Rj.jaip. bharbhar ‘the noise made by the flying of a bird’ — H. phurr ‘whirring sound (of wings)’ — Sant. phur phur ‘making buzzing, whirring sounds’ (one of Bodding’s examples is with a quail). There is certainly an onomatopoeic component in this lemma and it is unclear to which extend the Tibetan verb was borrowed into surrounding languages. Note also Pers. parper ‘fluttering’, and there are more similar Munda forms: reflexes of Proto-Kherwarian apir ‘to fly’ are found in several modern Munda languages and in Nih. aphir ‘to fly’ (Pinnow [K 501]). Whether or not there is IE influence in this lemma is difficult to say. Influence of OIA *spharati¹ ‘throbs, quivers’ (13820) and of sphuráti¹ ‘spurns, darts’ (13849)  can be excluded because of the different semantic reflexes in Bng. phɔrphɔrāṇɔ ‘to whirl or swirl up (as wind)’ and phurṇɔ ‘to twitch, bat (eye[lash], muscle)’. But it is clear that it is another example of what Mallory and Adams (already quoted above p. 778) describe as an instance “where onomatopoeia has supported their survival.” Cf. also PN *pʰar- ‘to flutter, fly’ (CINCL 101), PAA *par ‘to fly’ (also reflected in PMU **pER) and even Swab. pfurren ‘to flare up with whooshing, buzzing speed’ (von Schmid).

accepted.evidence: Zoller pp.823–824 records Kurux pəpəla butterfly alongside the Kurux paplā citation and Pfeiffer’s *papla comparison. DEDR4083(a) explicitly gives Kurux paplā. The shared p-p-l sequence and identical sense support a qualified family proposal; retain the extra schwa and final quantity difference, and the source’s expressive/areal caveat.

This matches the Dravidian article family; independent inheritance versus areal transmission is not settled by the match.

record.Etymology: 149. Bng. migṇɔ n.m. ‘(quick) blinking (with eyes)’ (with -ṇɔ2 suffix), e.g. seu migṇɔ kɔrɛ ‘he blinks’ (lit.‘he does blinking’), and miṅg-miṅg gaṛṇɔ ‘to blink (with the eyes)’ (with gaṛṇɔ ‘to pull out’) — Klm. ečämik HL n.f. ‘wink or blink of the eye’ (← ec̣ H(L) ‘eyes’) cf. PIE *meigʰ- (perhaps also *meik-) ‘close the eyes’. Sub OIA *micc- ‘close the eyes, blink’ (10118) there are also modern reflexes with -kk- extensions like H. mickānā ‘to wink’; according to Turner, “[a] non-Aryan or widespread onom. word, scarcely. . . to be assigned to a common IE. root. . . ” See also EWA sub MEṢ ‘to open the eyes’ (CDIAL MIṢ *‘blink, open the eyes’) regarding the complexity of this lemma and note also Dravidian Kurkh. miṅkh- ‘to close the eyes’ (Pfeiffer [1972: 28]). Directly related to 10118 are Bng. miċṇɔ ‘to blink; to close one’s eyes’ and mɔċrɔ2 ‘blinking (with eyes)’ (not to be confused with almost identically pronounced mɔċrɔ1 ‘drunk’ which is < OIA matsará- ‘exhilarating’ [9756] [Pa., Pk.] without known modern parallels). Since it is quite impossible that Bng. migṇɔ or miṅg-miṅg gaṛṇɔ is a -kk- extension of miċṇɔ, we have here yet another case of semantic-morphological amalgamations with the Bng. and Klm. forms closest to PIE. Regarding Bng. miṅg- miṅg gaṛṇɔ cf. e.g. Lith. mingù ‘to fall asleep’ (or rather miñga ‘falls asleep’) and see Derksen’s discussion of Proto-Baltic *migla ‘mist, haze’ and *migti ‘fall asleep’ (2015: 317).

accepted.evidence: DEDR4877 gives Kurux mīŋxnā close the eyes alongside Malto minqe and Kolami minpeŋ wink. Zoller pp.840–841 quotes the Kurux stem miŋkh- from Pfeiffer with the same meaning. Preserve short i versus dictionary ī and kh versus x notation; the stem-only citation excludes the infinitive ending. The wider Indo-European comparison is not asserted.

record.Etymology: 1670. Chin. huḍ ‘ewe’ and Paṭṭ. huṛ ‘ram, male sheep’ < OIA eḍa- ‘a kind of sheep’ (2512) (Pa., Pk.) with modern reflexes in the northwest, in S. and Si. Spontaneous aspiration also in Niya Prakrit heḍˈi ‘sheep(?)’ and in Brah. hēṭ ‘she-goat’. But the vowel is unclear. Note that the lemma with initial aspiration has also been borrowed into Psht. heṛə́y ‘sheep with a long tail’ (Cheung [2013: 626, fn. 37]).

accepted.evidence: DEDR5152 explicitly records Brahui hēṭ she-goat alongside Kurux ēṛā and Malto éṛe. Zoller p.743 instead relates hēṭ to OIA eḍa2512 with spontaneous aspiration, while noting a vowel difficulty; DEDR also compares Sanskrit eḍa without asserting a donor direction. record.Etymology: 40. Pal. keriˈšpīka ‘spark’; Kal. kuluspík (also kulušpík, kulišpík) ‘sparks, flying ember’; Dm. kiliˈṣpik; Pr. anig išpīg ‘spark’ are probably compounds with first element re- lated with the ‘(char)coal’ words discussed p. 768 sub Jaun. kuluṇɔ ‘to singe’ (except Pr. which reflects agní- ‘fire’); second element is probably cognate with Sak. ṣpargga- ‘noise, twang’ which reflects PIE *spr̥ə̑-g- ‘crackle, sputter’. These old compounds thus appear to have an original meaning like ‘live coal spatter’. They must not necessarily be Iranian borrowings. Notes: (a) Similar looking OIA sphuliṅga- ‘spark’ is not a cognate of the above forms. In KEWA Mayrhofer quotes Burrow who suggests relation with PIE *spr̥ə̑-g-; he rightly does not repeat this suggestion in EWA. This sphuliṅga- is part of a complex and not very transparent word field with elements of Indo-Aryan and Austro-Asiatic roots. In Zoller (2018: 337ff.) I have attempted to disentangle this complex. (b) Partly similar Brah. prišk ‘spark’ and Orm. spōx ‘live coal’ are difficult to connect here.

accepted.evidence: DEDR4191 explicitly records Brahui prishk spark alongside Pengo pṛiski, Manda pṛihe/pṛihki and Kuwi pṛiska/pṛisi. Zoller p.792 prints priśk spark and says it is difficult to connect with his wider Indo-Aryan spark group. The dictionary’s sh and source ś are retained as transcription variants; the exact Brahui family attestation supports4191 without endorsing the separate regional comparison.

record.Etymology: 1. The Bangāṇī God of Thunder is called guṛku (also meaning ‘thunder’) which is < OIA *guḍ- ‘rumble’ (4180) with a modern parallel in S. to which have to be added Thar. gurgurāi ‘thunder’, Kann. gŭrgŭr ‘thunder’, K. gur-gur ‘a rumble, thunder’ and gagrāy, gɨgrāray ‘thunder’ (Sachdeva et al. [2010: 56]), Klm. āga-guṛant HL-LH ‘it is thundering’ (lit. ‘the sky is thundering’), Garh. gagṛāṭ and giṛaktāḷ ‘thunder’, Ko.S. guḍguḍu ‘thunderbolt’, Ko.kaṇ. guḍguḍ ‘thunder’, and M. gaḍagaḍaṇeṃ ‘to thunder’ — Sant. guɖ guɖ ‘droning, rolling, rumbling (sound of thunder, railway, drums, a running flock of animals, of a water cataract)’, Gtaˈ guɽuŋ-geɽeeke ‘thunder’ — Ora. guṛguṛnā ‘thunder’.
